description.text: Francesco Crispi was born on 4 October 1818 in Ribera, Sicily, into an Albanian‑Sicilian family that traced its roots to the Arbëreshë settlers of the 15th century.  Educated first at a local seminary and later at the University of Palermo, he became a lawyer and a passionate advocate for the rights of the poor, publishing early works that criticized the excesses of the Church and called for equality before the law.

Crispi rose to national prominence as a leader of the 1848 Sicilian revolution and later as a key organizer of Giuseppe Garibaldi’s Expedition of the Thousand.  He served four terms as Italy’s Prime Minister, championed anti‑clerical reforms such as the Zanardelli Code that abolished the death penalty, pursued an aggressive colonial policy in Africa, and ultimately saw his government collapse after the disastrous defeat at Adua in 1896.  He died in Naples on 11 August 1901.

curiosities.text: Crispi was the first southern Italian to hold the office of Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Italy.
He played a pivotal role in the 1848 Sicilian revolution, organizing the defense committee and later joining Garibaldi’s forces in the Expedition of the Thousand.
As Minister of the Interior, Crispi introduced the Zanardelli Code, which abolished the death penalty and formally recognized the right to strike.
